draft.title: Responses of religious traditions
card: Dialogue
Religious groups talk and listen with non-religious people, such as humanists, to understand each other and find shared concerns. The aim is mutual understanding, not winning a debate.
Outreach
Religious groups reach out to people who have no religion. They may share their beliefs, run community programs or invite people to take part in their activities.
Adapting
Religious groups may change how they engage with society. They may use social media, hold services online, or use plainer language so more people can connect with them.
A tradition may use more than one response at the same time. These responses are about how it relates to non-religion, and they do not require it to change its core beliefs.
draft.remember: Religions can respond to non-religion by talking, reaching out and changing how they engage.

a.q: A church invites local humanists to a panel to discuss shared concerns such as caring for the poor. Which response is this?
a.why: The church and humanists talk and listen to each other to build understanding. That is dialogue. It is not outreach, because the aim is not to bring people into the church.
a.clue: The two groups talk and listen to each other.

b.q: A mosque in Sydney livestreams its talks and uses everyday English so people with little religious background can follow. Which response is this most clearly?
opts: Adapting how it engages with society
Changing its core beliefs to fit society
Outreach through a charity food program
b.why: Livestreaming and plainer language change the way the mosque engages with society, so this is adapting. It is not dialogue, as no non-religious group takes part in a conversation. Nothing here suggests a change in core beliefs.
b.clue: Look at what changed: the method, not the beliefs.

b.best: Adapting how it engages with society

problems.detail: The card's outreach includes inviting people to take part in a group's activities, and the church here invites humanists to its panel. The why rules out outreach because 'the aim is not to bring people into the church', but the card never defines outreach by that aim. Students get no card-based way to separate the two, beyond the 'shared concerns' wording.

check.summary: Both answers are clear and correct: dialogue for (a), adapting for (b). One minor issue: the why for (a) separates dialogue from outreach using an aim the card never states, while the card's outreach includes inviting people to activities.

proposal.title: Responses of religious traditions
card: Dialogue

A two-way exchange. Religious groups and non-religious people, such as humanists, each speak and listen to understand each other and find shared concerns. The aim is mutual understanding, not winning a debate.
Outreach
A one-way offer. A religious group goes out to people who have no religion and offers them something: its beliefs, community programs or a chance to join its activities.
Adapting
Religious groups may change how they engage with society. They may use social media, hold services online, or use plainer language so more people can connect with them.
A tradition may use more than one response at the same time. These responses are about how it relates to non-religion, and they do not require it to change its core beliefs.
proposal.remember: Dialogue listens both ways, outreach offers one way, and adapting changes the method, not the core beliefs.

a.q: A church and a local humanist group meet each month. Each side explains its views and listens to the other's. Which response is this?
a.why: Both groups speak and listen to understand each other, so this is a two-way exchange: dialogue. It is not outreach, because outreach is one way, with the church offering its beliefs, programs or activities to others.
a.clue: Does the talking go one way or both ways?

b.clue: Look at what changed: the method, not the beliefs.
